comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C12-C13 describing the two illustrative examples from Figure 1. Both evaluations find these examples well-supported and note they effectively demonstrate the manuscript's argument about problems with the non-significance criterion.

Perfect agreement on claims C14-C15, C53-C55 describing equivalence testing methodology. Both evaluations accept the methodological framework without question, with peer reviewers describing it as providing 'a superior quantitative framework.'

Perfect agreement on claims C70-C72 regarding the conceptual distinction between Bayes factors and equivalence tests. Both evaluations accept that these methods address different questions and are complementary rather than competing approaches.

Agreement on claims C34-C35 regarding RPP/EPRP analysis, though OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative explanation and limited sample size ('merely anecdotal'), while peer reviewers accept without challenge as part of broader 'significant insights.'

Perfect agreement on claims C26-C27, C81 explaining why non-significance is common even with adequate power. Both evaluations accept this as well-established principle, with peer reviewer explicitly endorsing the reasoning.
Perfect agreement on claims C36-C38 regarding methodological recommendations for study design and pre-registration. Both evaluations accept these as standard best practices without challenge.

Perfect agreement on claims C82-C85 regarding interpretation guidance and avoiding arbitrary dichotomization. Peer reviewer initially raised concerns but accepted the authors' clarification in revision, aligning with OpenEval's positive assessment.

Perfect agreement on claims C90-C94 acknowledging limitations and alternative approaches. Both evaluations accept these as appropriate scholarly caution, with peer reviewers focusing praise on implemented methods.

Strong agreement on claims C74-C78, C87-C88 presenting main conclusions and recommendations. Both evaluations strongly endorse these claims, with peer reviewers calling it a 'valuable contribution' and OpenEval finding them well-supported by the analyses. Minor difference: R17 includes C89 which R12 does not explicitly address.

Strong agreement on conceptual critique of non-significance criterion (C2-C3, C6-C7, C10, C50-C52). Both evaluations accept the logical arguments based on statistical principles. Peer review groups these with C1 and C5 (methodological descriptions), while OpenEval separates those into R1.

Strong agreement on claims C39-C40, C86 comparing the two approaches and recommending both be used together. Both evaluations accept the complementary nature, with peer reviewer explicitly endorsing 'using both methods as suggested.' OpenEval includes C41 (Bayes factor interpretation) which peer review addresses separately.

Strong agreement on Bayes factor methodology (C19-C22, C65). Both evaluations accept the framework without challenge. OpenEval includes C41 (interpretation rules) which peer review addresses in R11. Peer review includes C68-C69 (prior choice) which OpenEval addresses in R10.

Strong agreement on main empirical findings (C4, C73, C79-C80) showing contrast between 73% non-significance rate and <40% with principled methods. Both evaluations strongly endorse the reanalysis. Peer review groups these with detailed reanalysis results (C9, C16-C18, C23-C25, C67) which OpenEval addresses separately.

Agreement on Bayesian reanalysis results (C23-C25, C67). OpenEval addresses these with prior choice justification (C68-C69) in R10, while peer review groups them with broader reanalysis findings in R2. Both find the analysis well-supported.

Agreement on equivalence testing reanalysis results (C16-C18). OpenEval groups these with additional claims (C28-C29, C57-C59) in R7, while peer review includes them in broader reanalysis endorsement in R2. Both evaluations accept the findings.

Agreement on sensitivity analyses (C32-C33). OpenEval addresses these with broader sensitivity analysis context (C30-C31, C60-C62) in R8, while peer review focuses specifically on C32-C33 in R6. Both accept the analyses as supporting the main findings.

Agreement on factual RPCB results (C9, C45-C48). OpenEval groups these together in R4, while peer review includes them with broader methodological descriptions (C8, C42-C44, C49) in R14. Both accept these as accurate empirical observations.

Agreement on factual descriptions of replication project methodology (C1, C5, C8, C42-C44). OpenEval addresses these in R1, while peer review groups them with RPCB success rates (C45-C48) and recommendations (C49) in R14. Both accept as accurate characterizations.

Partial overlap on C1 and C5 (factual descriptions of replication projects). OpenEval groups these with C8, C42-C44 in R1, while peer review groups C1 and C5 with conceptual critique (C2-C3, C6-C7, C10, C50-C52) in R1. Both find claims supported.

Agreement on methodological recommendation C49 regarding multiple replication indicators. OpenEval addresses this alone in R19, while peer review includes it with broader factual descriptions in R14. Both accept as representing consensus in replication literature.

OpenEval addresses C11 (statistical property of requiring significance in both studies) as well-established and supported by citation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; this technical detail may have been accepted implicitly as part of broader methodological framework.
